title: Place value and decimals: longer is not larger
hook: "0.45 is bigger than 0.6 because 45 is bigger than 6." This is one of the most common errors in primary maths, and it lasts into high school if nobody fixes it.
coreIdeaMd:
Place value works the same way on both sides of the decimal point: each place is **ten times** the place to its right.

- Tenths are bigger than hundredths, just as tens are bigger than ones.
- To compare decimals, compare the **largest place first**, not the number of digits.
- Writing a zero to make the lengths match ($0.6 = 0.60$) helps students see this.

Use place value charts, money (dollars, 10-cent and 1-cent coins) and number lines.
workedExampleMd:
**Which is larger, $0.38$ or $0.5$?**

| | Ones | Tenths | Hundredths |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.38 | 0 | 3 | 8 |
| 0.5 | 0 | 5 | 0 |

1. Compare the ones: both 0.
2. Compare the tenths: 5 is more than 3.
3. So $0.5 > 0.38$. The 8 hundredths can't make up for 2 missing tenths.

In money: 50 cents is more than 38 cents.

checkItems.feedbackCorrect: Yes. 7 tenths is more than 2 tenths, so 0.7 is larger, whatever comes after.
checkItems.feedbackIncorrect: Compare the tenths first: 0.7 has 7 tenths and 0.25 has 2. So 0.7 is larger. In money, 70 cents beats 25 cents.

wrongAnswers.feedback: 25 is bigger than 7 as a whole number, but here the digits are in different places. Write 0.7 as 0.70: 70 hundredths is more than 25 hundredths.

tryTomorrow: Write five decimals of different lengths on cards (for example 0.6, 0.45, 0.405, 0.5, 0.08) and ask groups to order them, then explain the hardest pair.
reflectPrompt: Which of your students might be comparing decimals by length? How would you find out in one question?
